title: The son who asked why
hookLine: Devavrata asks his grieving father why, hears half an answer, and quietly finds the rest: pitru devo bhava
carry: pitru devo bhava: honor your father as god
last: KAMA IS HONORED, BUT DHARMA COMES FIRST.

cards: Devavrata, the heir, has watched his father grow quiet and pale, sitting lost in thought, and he can't find a reason for it anywhere. The kingdom is at peace, and nothing is missing that he can see.

So the son does something that takes a little nerve with a king. He stands before him and asks straight out: everything in the kingdom is going well, so why are you grieving? And Shantanu answers him.

teach.h: ONE SON IS LIKE NO SON.
teach.b: Here is Shantanu's answer, in the text's sense. You are my only son, and the wise say a man with one son is like a man with none. You're a warrior, always among weapons.
If you fell in battle, what would become of our line? Every word of it is something the king could mean. But it isn't the whole reason he's grieving, and the text lets us see that.
He can't say: I want a woman whose father demands your crown. Devavrata doesn't argue.
He goes to someone who would know, an old minister devoted to his father, and asks. And the old man tells him: the fisherman's daughter by the Yamuna, and her father's condition.

teach.h: HE THINKS OF WHAT HE CAN DO.
teach.b: Now notice what the son doesn't do. He doesn't confront his father, or sulk about a crown he might lose. He starts to think about what he can do for him.
Hindu tradition holds Bhishma up for exactly this. The Taittiriya Upanishad gives students lines to carry when they leave their teacher's house.
One is for the mother, and the next is pitru devo bhava: let your father be like God to you.
Many teachers read it this way: not that a father is always right, but that a parent's well-being is sacred, worth your time, your attention, even your own sacrifice.
That's seva, loving service, and it's why in many Hindu homes grown children care for aging parents, touch their feet, and keep them close.
Devavrata hears a half answer, and instead of feeling shut out, he goes looking for what his father couldn't say.

how: Many Hindus touch the feet of parents and elders to receive their blessing, and caring for aging parents is treated as a child's sacred duty; retellings hold Bhishma up as an example of it.

o: the king's promise to keep his only son out of every battle
a son's promise, which starts with him hearing his father's half answer
a minister's oath to keep the king's secret from the heir

games.q: the king's grief — tap the pairs.
p: told the son the real reason
let your father be like God

s: Shantanu told his son the whole truth
he spoke of fears for the family line, not of the fisherman's daughter.
pitru devo bhava means a father is always right
many teachers read it as treating a parent's well-being as sacred, worth your own care.
Devavrata met his father's grief by looking for a way to help
he didn't confront him; he found the real reason and began to think what he could do.

games.q: you're Devavrata. your father is grieving, and the reason he gives you doesn't quite fit. what do you do?
o: accept his answer and let it go.
quietly ask the old minister who serves him.
games.why: he goes to an old minister devoted to his father and learns the real reason, so he can help. his father's sorrow is his business: pitru devo bhava.

practice: Bring to mind a parent or elder who has cared for you, living or gone. If it's your way, picture yourself touching their feet, the way many Hindus greet parents and elders, and receiving their blessing.

Breathe in their care for you; breathe out one small thing you could do for them this week: a call, a cup of chai, an hour of listening. If no parent comes to mind, hold any elder who has been family to you.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma's vow. Before the vow, a son who hears his father's half answer, and goes to find the rest.

orig.note: Sanskrit pitṛdevo bhava, let your father be like God to you: from the Taittiriya Upanishad (1.11).

carryVoice: Your line: pitru devo bhava, honor your father as God. Next, a prince at a fisherman's door. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Devavrata asks his father; Shantanu's answer; the old minister reveals the cause)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (pitru devo bhava: let your father be like God to you)
